div.p: Real-time systems used in media processing and transmission produce bursty workloads with highly variable execution and transmission times. To avoid the drawbacks of using the worst-case approach with these workloads, this paper uses a variation of the usual real-time task model where the WCET is replaced by a discrete statistical distribution. Using this approach, tasks are characterized by their processing time over a sampling period. We could expect that increasing the sampling period would smooth, in principle, the workload variability and the proposed analysis would provide more deterministic longterm results. However, we have surprisingly observed that this variability does not decreases with the sampling period: workloads are bursty on many time scales. This property is known as self-similarity and is measured using the Hurst parameter.

This paper studies how to properly model and analyze selfsimilar task sets showing the influence of the Hurst parameter on the schedulability analysis. It shows, through an analytical model and simulations, that this parameter may have a very negative impact on system performance. As a conclusion, it can be stated that this factor should be taken into account for statistical analysis of real-time systems, since simplistic workload models can lead to inaccurate results. It also shows that the negative effect of this parameter can be bounded using scheduling policies based on the bandwidth isolation principle.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Understanding the nature of the workload is critical to properly modeling a real-time system. The simplest way of characterizing the execution time of a real-time task is by describing it with its WCET (Worst-Case Execution Time). The analysis of hard real-time systems is only based on this parameter. However, in multimedia and network based realtime systems, workloads are highly variable and the WCET approach faces important drawbacks, like the problem of accurately determining the WCET poor resource utilization. Several statistical characterizations and analysis methods have been proposed for these systems [1]- [4], but they have not taken into account the self-similar nature of media workloads.

Self-similarity characterizes the fact that a workload is not only highly variable, but it is also variable bursty on many time scales or, in other words, the burst behaviour may itself be bursty. This makes real-time tasks that exhibit this behavior even more difficult to characterize using simplistic models like the WCET or discrete statistical distributions. This paper analyses in which situations the workload of a real-time system can be regarded as self-similar and studies its impact on the schedulability analysis.

In the last decade it was stated that network traffic shows two properties [5], [6]: i) self-similarity: counts of packet arrivals in equally-spaced intervals of time are long-range, time-dependent and have a large coefficient of deviation; and ii) heavy-tailed: packet inter-arrival times have a marginal distribution that has a longer tail than the exponential distribution. Several distributions have been proposed to fit these traffic characteristics. The Pareto and Weibull distributions are often used to reflect the heavy-tailed distribution.

Studies have shown that CPU requirements of Unix processes are self-similar and have heavy-tailed distributions [7]- [9]. This finding was very important in the world of scheduling because it meant that scheduling policies had to be reevaluated in terms of their behaviour on these highly-variable and heavytailed workloads [10]. Multimedia streams also exhibit selfsimilar properties with Hurst values between 0.75 and 0.95 [11], [12].

Self-similar computations are more and more common in real-time systems, mainly in applications related to media transmission and signal processing. The causes for highly bursty and variable processing times include real-time transmission of video and other high-bandwidth sensors, use of non-deterministic networks and protocols (like Ethernet and TCP/IP), real-time processing of images through complex algorithms (like pattern recognition, image filtering,...), and cache memories.

The main question about self-similarity is "what are the implications of self-similarity on real-time systems performance?". The effect of self-similarity has been already studied in network traffic [13]- [16]. These works show that packet losses and delays are radically different when simulations use either real traffic data or synthetic data that have long-range dependence. The effect on non real-time scheduling has been also studied in [9], [17].

This paper addresses the study of the influence of selfsimilar workload on real-time scheduling. Real-time tasks with variable execution times will be modeled using an "on-off" model [18] where the "on" state represents time intervals where the task is active and the "off" state represents the intervals of task inactivity. Such a set of tasks behaves sta-Fig. 1: Multimedia pipeline processing tistically as a fractional Brownian motion (fBm), which is the base for our analytical schedulability analysis. Results show the dependency of schedulability on the Hurst parameter. Furthermore, in a set of periodic and aperiodic tasks, the aperiodic workload can seriously jeopardize the schedulability of periodic tasks. Analytical results are further checked and confirmed via simulations. The study allows us to conclude that a bandwidth isolation or reservation mechanism (such as the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [19]) is recommended for environments with a mix of hard-deadline periodic tasks and soft-deadline sporadic tasks.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: section II introduces the model and assumptions of real-time system used in this paper; section III reviews the concepts and definitions of self-similarity and heavy-tailed distributions; section IV presents the basic "on-off" model and its application to modeling real-time tasks; section V contains the schedulability analysis; section VI evaluates the influence of self-similarily on the EDF (Earliest Deadline First) scheduler, and finally; section VII presents some concluding remarks.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The model of real-time systems assumed in this work was originally devised in the scope of multimedia transmission and processing, although it can be generalized to task systems with highly variable processing times. In these systems, the worst-case execution time is difficult to estimate and does not characterize tasks properly.

Computations in a media processing system are usually structured in a pipeline fashion as shown in Figure 1. Data are produced continuously by media sources (encoders) at highly variable rates. Each task of the pipeline reads data, processes it and sends it to the next task. Tasks are interconnected through buffers. The last task of a pipeline is usually a media player, and its input buffer is usually known as the playback buffer. Such a system is a mix of periodic and aperiodic/sporadic tasks. Aperiodic tasks, such as video encoding and video processing, are usually data-driven. They are triggered by data with highly variable interarrival times. Periodic tasks, such as video rendering, are strictly periodic, but their computation time is highly variable. Periods are usually related to applica-tion parameters, like video frame frequency or audio sampling period. Buffers play a key role in these systems: they allow to connect periodic and aperiodic tasks asynchronously.

div.head: A. Task model
div.p: The task model proposed for the above system is really a statistical extension of the classical real-time task model. The model assumes a mix of periodic and aperiodic/sporadic tasks with the following attributes:
• Periodic tasks:
div.formula: P i (C i , T i , D i )
div.p: , where C i is the computation time, T i is the period, and D i is the deadline. • Sporadic tasks: S i (C i , I i , D i ): where C i and D i are defined in the same way as for periodic tasks, and I i is the task inter-arrival time. This model only differs from the classical real-time model in the fact that C i is not the worst-case execution time (WCET) but a statistical distribution. More precisely, C i is defined as the intensity or CPU utilization of a task over a given sampling period. Analogously, the inter-arrival time I i is also a statistical distribution. Statistical characterizations were used by the authors of this paper in previous studies [4], [20] and also by other authors [1], [2], [21]. However, the novelty of this paper is properly modeling self-similar workloads using heavy-tailed distributions and extending task characterization with the inclusion of the Hurst parameter.

The rationale for using statistical distributions in task modeling and the importance of the Hurst parameter is illustrated with a real example of a Unix computer processing video images. Figure 2a shows the trace of the CPU utilization captured using DTrace. The trace represents the CPU utilization during a sampling period of 0.04s. The system comprises 8 tasks: 6 periodic tasks and 2 aperiodic tasks. Figure 2b shows the workload distribution for three different sampling periods: 0.04, 0.4, and 2s. Table I shows the average computation time, its variance, and the distribution tail value (.99-quantile), for the above periods. The variance and the tail value have been "normalized" by multiplying them by the quotient between the sampling period and 0.04s, so they can be comparable to the first sampling period. We could expect that increasing the sampling period would smooth, in principle, the workload variability so we could apply more conventional analysis methods and obtain more deterministic long-term results. However, we surprisingly observed that this variability did not decrease with the sampling period. It can be shown that, although, the mean value is the same, the variance increases with the sampling period more than expected 1 . This reflects that the workload is bursty on many time scales or self-similar. Finally, we calculated the Hurst parameter of this workload and is 0.73.
How to properly model such a self-similar workload, the effect of the sampling period and the Hurst parameter on schedulability is further anlyzed in the following sections.

div.head: III. BACKGROUND ON SELF-SIMILARITY
div.p: The analysis of stationary time series data or stochastic processes can reveal the property of self-similarity. This is 1 For a white noise the normalized variance would remain constant. 2a the case, for example, of the CPU utilization over a sampling period. This has been well studied in network traffic.

div.head: A. Definition of Self-Similarity
div.p: A phenomenon that is self-similar looks the same at different scales on a dimension. This means that at different time scales (microseconds, milliseconds, seconds) the statistical properties are similar.

More formally, let {X t : t = 0, 1, 2, . . .} ({X t } for short) be a discrete stationary stochastic process representing the evolution in time of a statistical distribution (for example, the workload of a system). Let σ 2 be the variance and let r(k) = Cov(X t , X t+k )/σ 2 be the autocorrelation function of {X t }. We define {X (m) t } as the m-aggregated process of {X t }, which is obtained by aggregating and averaging the data in X t by blocks of size m:

Aggregating really means multiplying the sampling period by a factor m. An important effect of the process aggregation is to smooth the traffic rate in each period. Therefore, the variation is reduced. The question of how this variation changes depending on the aggregation factor is related to the study of the self-similarity of a process. A process is distributionally self-similar if the processes {X t } and {X (m) t } have the same distribution, up to a scaling factor. A self-similar process has the property that, when it is aggregated, the new process has the same autocorrelation function as the original one. Formally, the process {X t } is called second-order selfsimilar with Hurst parameter

If the second condition only holds when m → ∞, then a process is asymptotically second-order self-similar. If 0 < H < 0.5, the process is Short-Range Dependent (SRD), and if 0.5 < H < 1, the process is Long-Range Dependent (LRD).
The variance of the m-aggregated process is obtained as:

div.head: B. Fractional Brownian Motion
div.p: A common way to model self-similar processes is using a fractional Brownian model. The fractional Brownian motion (denoted fBm) model can be viewed as an extension of the standard Brownian Motion models that have been used in heavy traffic analysis. Formally, the normalized fractional Brownian motion {Z H (t) : t ≥ 0} is a continuous zero mean Gaussian process with stationary increments and variance |t| 2H . The correlation of the increments is characterized by the Hurst index, H. Unlike the standard Brownian motion, the fractional one has a long-range dependency property when H > 1/2. div.head: C. Heavy-tailed distributions
div.p: A distribution is heavy-tailed if

Heavy-tailed distributions have a number of properties that are different from exponential or normal distributions. If α ≤ 2, then the distribution has an infinite variance; if α ≤ 1, then the distribution has an infinite mean. Thus, as α decreases, a larger portion of the probabilistic mass function may be present in the tail of the distribution. In practical terms, a random variable that follows a heavy-tailed distribution can have extremely large values with nonnegligible probability.
The simplest heavy-tailed distribution is the Pareto distribution:

where d is the minimal value of the distribution and α is known as the Pareto index. The problem with using the Pareto distribution is its infinite variance. This poses problems when simulating a system with heavy-tailed distributions. Specifically, in [23], it is shown that simulations become infeasible for α < 1.5. A practical approach for solving this problem is to bound the Pareto distribution [24]. A Bounded-Pareto distribution is characterized by three parameters: the Pareto index α, the minimal value d, and the largest value p:

It is easy to see that if p is very high, the distribution is very similar to the unbounded one. Therefore, for large values of p it can be assumed that it is heavy-tailed [24]. Finally, note that self-similarity as well as heavy-tailed distributions are convenient mathematical idealizations and can never be fully validated from finite data sets. However, these idealizations are powerful mathematical tools for modeling important aspects of time series.

div.head: IV. AN "ON-OFF" MODEL FOR REAL-TIME COMPUTATIONS
div.p: Real-time computations with variable execution times can be modeled as an "on-off" process. This model is based on a proposal of [25] originally by Mandelbrot [18]. This method consists of superimposing many simple "on-off" streams where the "on" and "off" periods strictly alternate. The resulting process is self-similar and statistically behaves as a fractional Brownian motion under certain requirements on the distributions of the "on" and "off" states.

Simple "on-off" models are commonly used to describe the random nature of the network traffic [23], [25]. In network models, the source transmits the packet in the "on" state, while the "off" state represents the inter-arrival time. For real-time systems, we propose modeling the arrival of a task instance (or job) by the start of the "on" state, and modeling task computing times by the duration of this "on" state. The "off" state represents the inter-arrival time between successive jobs. The "on" and "off" states strictly alternate. Figure 3, shows a system example with 3 tasks. The first job of task one arrives at time 1 with an expected execution of 3.8 time units. The next arrival of this task is at time 9.1 with execution time 2. The first job of task two, arrives at time 1.9 and has an expected execution time of 2.5. Note that this model reflects the arrival and execution times of the jobs and not when the jobs are executed (this will depend on the scheduler).

div.head: B. Modeling real-time tasks
div.p: Real-time systems for media processing are a mix of periodic and aperiodic/sporadic tasks. Usually, these tasks are connected in a pipeline fashion as described in section II. Periodic tasks are modeled using a t on which corresponds to the computation time and t of f = Tt on . Some periodic tasks, like video playing, have heavy-tailed distributions for execution times. Some other periodic tasks may have variable execution times but not necessarily heavy-tailed. Table II shows possible distributions. However, even when execution times are modeled with heavy-tailed distributions, the workload that they generate cannot be assured, in principle, to be self-similar. This is because the "off" period is not independent of the "on" period. Being independent is a sufficient condition (but not necessary) of Theorems 1 and 2 for self-similarity. Nevertheless, practical experiments show that periodic streams with the "on" (or "off") period Pareto distributed are selfsimilar.

Aperiodic tasks are data-driven and t of f corresponds to the inter-arrival distribution of data. In tasks associated with network traffic, the inter-arrival distribution is heavy-tailed. On the other hand, data processing is also heavy-tailed and independent from the inter-arrival distribution. Therefore, using theorem 2, aperiodic tasks generate self-similar workload.

As an example, let's make a synthetic workload model for the real system described in section II. The goal is to obtain a workload model that has first-order (mean) and secondorder (self-similarity) statistics properties that are equivalent to the workload trace shown in Figure 2a. The model has 6 periodic tasks and 2 sporadic tasks. The most important task is P 1 , which models a task that processes a video stream. Sporadic tasks (S 1 and S 2 ) are associated with network streams and, thus, their inter-arrival distributions are heavytailed. We generated a workload trace for a time of 1600s with a period of 0.04s. The result was similar to the traffic trace of Figure 2a. The mean utilization of this workload trace is 0.45. Figure 5 shows the variance time plot of the workload using a base period of 0.01s. The slope of the line corresponds to a Hurst parameter of 0.72, which allows us to state that the workload generated is self-similar. III (Base period for m=1 is 0.01s). The Hurst parameter is 0.72.

div.head: V. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: In performance evaluation of network systems, there has been clear evidence of the practical importance of the Hurst parameter. In particular, the work in [13], [14], [28] demonstrates a significant difference in queueing performance (expressed in terms of queue length distribution) from traditional (Markovian) traffic models. In practice, not accounting for the self-similar property of the workload can lead to optimistic performance predictions.

The analysis described in this section can be summarized as follows: i) we set a utilization bound (U (t) < B) for determining the schedulability of the workload model; ii) as stated by Theorem 1 (and 2) the "on-off" workload model behaves statistically as the fractional Brownian motion arrival process A * (t) described by equation 13; iii) using A * (t), we obtain an expression of the current pending workload C(t), that is known as the fractional Brownian storage model; iv) Since U (t) can be expressed using C(t), we can evaluate the tail behavior for obtaining the schedulability probability: P (U (t) > D • B). The evaluation of this expression clearly shows that schedulability depends on the Hurst factor.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: The effect of heavy-tailed sources for non real-time scheduling disciplines has recently been studied. The main interest in these studies is to evaluate the response times (sojourn times) for heavy-tailed and self-similar workloads (for example, for web server applications). In [9], it was shown that First Come First Served (FCFS), as well as any other non-preemptive scheduling disciplines, performs very poorly since many jobs have to spend a long time in the system because one very large job is running. In contrast, Priority Sharing (PS) is optimal in providing a fair response time (in other words, if a job stays in the system for a long time, its the job's own fault) [17]. Although these results are obvious, new scheduling disciplines have been (re-)introduced in the context of web servers. A good example is the Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) [24], which is as optimal as PS. In several aspects, SRPT is very similar to EDF.

Our goal is to evaluate self-similar workload on real-time schedulers such as EDF. In the following experiments, we define several workload models. With these workload models we generate a sequence of jobs for a given time simulation. Each job is a tuple (t, i, C, D) representing the arrival time (t), task stream number (i), computation time (C) and deadline (D). Using this sequence, we simulated a preemptive EDF scheduler and obtained the deadline miss ratio, which is the proportion between the jobs that miss their deadlines and the total of jobs generated.

div.head: A. Heavy-tailed workload
div.p: All the experiments described in this subsection used a workload in which all the tasks were heavy-tailed distributed. The simulation time was 10,000s and each simulation was repeated 100 times in order to obtain 95% confidence intervals.

In the first set of experiments, we used a workload with a constant number of sporadic task streams (N = 10) and an execution time C i that was equally heavy-tailed distributed. In each experiment, we set a global workload utilization U and deadline D. Thus, the utilization of each stream was U i = U/N . The Hurst parameter H was varied from 0.5 to 0. 8. Note that the deadline miss ratio increases as the Hurst ratio increases. For Hurst parameters above 0.8, the ratio is significantly increased. The second curve shows the results for high workload and the same deadline (U = 0.9, D = 1). The results are very similar (although slightly higher). This means that the heavy-tail distribution has more impact on the deadline miss ratio than the workload utilization. That is, the jobs generated with execution times on the tail of the distribution (near 0.8s) are the jobs that missed their deadline. The third curve shows the deadline miss ratio with a more stringent deadline (U = 0.5, D = 0.1). Note that, in this case some jobs can never be scheduled because the deadline is lower than the maximal value p. Note that the loss ratio increases as the Hurst parameter increases.

In the previous experiment, the mean execution time ( Ci ) increases as the Hurst parameter increases. Consequently, the difference between deadline and execution time was reduced so more jobs missed their deadlines. In other words, the more heavy-tailed the task execution time, the greater the deadline miss ratio. This is an obvious result of the experiment.

A workload can be heavy-tailed (that is, with high variable execution times), but this does not implies being self-similar.. Thus, in the following set of experiments we evaluate EDF performance depending on the Hurst parameter isolating the effect of the heavy-tailed distribution of execution times. This way, we kept the execution time constant and the interarrival time was heavy-tailed distributed. Specifically, tasks have constant execution times (C i = C(0.1s)). This increase is more significant for Hurst values greater than 0.8.

The previous experiment reduced the minimal inter-arrival time (d) when the Hurst parameter increased. In this third set of experiments, the value of d was constant. In order to maintain the utilization constant independently of the Hurst value, the number of streams was varied. The results are shown in Figure 10. The first curve shows the deadline miss ratio for a utilization of 0.35 and a deadline of 0.05. Note that, for Hurst values greater than 0.6, the tasks start to miss their deadlines. For greater intensities (the other two lines), the ratio increases more slowly.

The results of the experiments presented in this subsection confirms the results of the schedulability analysis of Section V. The effect of the Hurst parameter is more important when the utilization of the workload is low (and consequently the ratio is low). When the utilization is high the influence of self-simililarity in the deadline miss ratio is reduced.

div.head: B. Mixed workload
div.p: The following experiment used a mixed set of tasks. The periodic set of tasks are the same as those in Table III except for P 1 (that is, all the non heavy-tailed tasks). The mean utilization of these periodic tasks is 0.142. For the heavy-tailed tasks, we generated 5 streams with a constant execution time (C i = C(0.1s)) and inter-arrival time A i Pareto distributed. The Pareto parameters were calculated in the same way as the previous experiments in order to maintain a utilization of 0.1 for each stream. The resulting mean utilization of the workload was 0.64. In the EDF simulation, we distinguished between heavy-tailed and non heavy-tailed tasks in order to obtain the deadline miss ratio. The results are shown in Figure 11. The results for the sporadic tasks ("SPORADIC" curve) show that the ratio increases when H is greater than 0.7. For the periodic tasks ("PERIODIC" curve), we can see that tasks miss their deadlines when the Hurst parameter is higher than 0.6. That is, increasing the self-similarity of the aperiodic task causes the loss of deadlines in the non heavy-tailed periodic tasks.

div.head: C. Self-similar Overload Management
div.p: We have seen that a workload with a Hurst index higher than 0.6 is more likely to produce transient overloads in a real-time system. Transient overloads can be handled through a resource reservation approach. A simple and effective mechanism for implementing temporal isolation under EDF is the Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [19]. A CBS is characterized by a budget c i , a dynamic server deadline d i , and by an ordered pair (Q i ; T i ), where Q i is the maximum budget and T i is the period of the server. The ratio U i = Q i /T i is denoted as the server bandwidth. CBS behaves as a work-conserving algorithm, exploiting the available slack in an efficient way.

An important property is that, in any interval of time of length L, a CBS with bandwidth U i will never demand more than U i L, independently of the actual task requests. This property allows the CBS to be used as a bandwidth reservation strategy in order to allocate a fraction of the CPU time to soft tasks whose computation time cannot be easily bounded.

We repeated the previous experiment assigning a server bandwidth to each task. For the periodic tasks, we assigned a utilization U i based on their WCET and the period T i . For the aperiodic tasks, we assigned a utilization based on their mean utilization. In the simulations performed, no periodic task missed its deadline and the sporadic tasks increased their deadline miss rate. The results of this ratio are shown in the curve "SPORADIC CBS" of Figure 11.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper studies the implications of self-similar workload in real-time systems. Workload that is bursty on many time scales can be described statistically using the concept of selfsimilarity. Self-similar workloads may appear in a real-time system in two main ways: the processing of multimedia and network streams, and in non-deterministic computations.

We have proposed a task workload model based on an "on-off" model that is self-similar. Using this model, we evaluated the influence of the Hurst parameter on the efficiency of the scheduler. First, analytical evaluation shows that selfsimililarity has a strong dependence on schedulability efficiency. Second, the experiments confirms this: increasing the Hurst parameter above 0.6 has a serious impact on the deadline miss ratio. For example, a system that performed correctly under non self-similar workload starts to miss deadlines when the Hurst parameter is increased. Furthermore, the self-similar workload also has an influence on periodic tasks. Thus, we need mechanisms of temporal isolation such as the CBS.

The consequences are very important for scheduling analysis, workload models and real-time systems simulation. We think that scheduling policies should be revised in order to correctly process self-similar workload.
